title: The force of imagination
hookLine: imagination can make us ill or well (Essays 1.21)
last: PITY MOVES SOME HEARTS, COURAGE MOVES OTHERS.

cards: A passenger on a plane starts scratching their head. Two minutes later, the passenger behind them is scratching too. Nothing has landed on that second head.
Only a picture in a mind has changed. Or someone at dinner describes a dentist's drill in detail, and around the table, jaws clench.
Montaigne noticed this in himself and gave it an essay, which opens on a Latin saying of the scholars: a strong imagination produces the event.

teach.b: First, the confession. Montaigne says plainly that he's one of the people imagination works on hardest. The sight of someone else's pain gives him a pain of his own.
A man who keeps coughing near him makes his own lungs and throat feel raw. It isn't a theory. It's a report on his body.

teach.h: A WOMAN AND A BENT PIN.
teach.b: He tells of a woman who was sure she'd swallowed a pin with her bread, and cried out that she could feel it stuck in her throat.
Someone sensible guessed it was her imagination, made her throw up, and slipped a bent pin into what came up. Seeing it, she felt her pain lift. Third, the doctors.
Physicians work on a patient's imagination too, Montaigne notes, winning belief with promises of a cure, so that imagination can do part of the work.
In this essay, imagination can make us ill, and it can help make us well. Fourth, his honesty about his stories.

teach.h: HE LEAVES TALES TO THEIR TELLERS.
teach.b: He admits he can't vouch for every tale he borrows, and leaves them on the conscience of whoever told them.

What matters to him is that they're possible, and that they show something true about how people are made. It's a careful line, and it fits the subject: an author who knows his own mind can run ahead of the facts.
In a plain week, the force of imagination is the email you've decided is angry before you open it. Montaigne's move is to notice: the mind is making a picture, and the body is believing it.

how: Readers of Montaigne turn to his essay on the force of imagination for its frank self-report: he describes how pictures in his own mind stir pain or relief in his body, and how others use that power.

games.q: what does “the force of imagination” mean?
o: an artist's gift for inventing new stories and pictures
how a picture in the mind can stir pain or ease in the body
the power to make wishes come true just by picturing them

games.q: the force of imagination: tap the pairs.
p: slipped in to end the woman's pain
left on the conscience of their tellers

s: Montaigne says imagination hardly affects him
he says he's one of the people imagination works on hardest.
in the story, a bent pin was slipped in to ease the woman's pain
someone guessed her pain came from imagination, and the pin she saw brought her relief.
Montaigne swears every story in the essay is true
he admits he can't vouch for all of them, and leaves them on the conscience of their tellers.

games.q: a woman is sure she swallowed a pin and feels it in her throat. you suspect it's her imagination. what does the person in Montaigne's story do?
o: tell her firmly she's imagining it.
make her throw up and slip a bent pin into what comes up.
ignore her until she calms down.
games.why: the pain lifted when she saw the pin. Montaigne tells it to show that what the mind believes, the body can feel.

practice: Bring to mind a lemon, yellow and cold from the fridge, cut in half with juice on the board, and notice what your mouth does.

Then bring to mind something you've been dreading this week, and notice your shoulders, stomach or jaw, though nothing in the room has changed. Name it quietly, it imagines, and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: The force of imagination. Montaigne's essay on how a picture in the mind can stir pain or ease in the body, starting with his own. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a strong imagination produces the event, the saying Montaigne opens this essay with.

carryVoice: Your line: it imagines. The picture can be vivid while the thing itself hasn't happened. See you tomorrow.
